Messages.Body:
The V:EKN is coordinating four invitational V:TES continental championship
tournaments in 2004, in Australia, Europe, North America, and South America.

To play in a championship tournament, players will first have to qualify by
finishing in the top 25% (rounded up) of the non-qualified players at one of
the qualifying tournaments. Qualifying in any qualifier enables a player to
play in any and all of the four continental championships. The finalists
from the 2003 championships are pre-qualified for the 2004 championships.

Once a player qualifies, he or she is free to play in other qualifiers (the
qualifiers are all open tournaments). But such previously-qualified players
do not count when determining the new qualifiers at that tournament.

For example, in a tournament with 25 non-qualified players and 6 previously-
qualified players, the top 7 non-qualified players (25/4 = 6.25 => 7) will
qualify, regardless of the finishing positions of the 6 previously-qualified
players.

http://www.white-wolf.com/vtes/Championship.html

Messages.Author: Jamie The Seppo

This is WAY too harsh for Australia.
It is great that by qualifying once you can go to any of the 4
continental championships, but this is absolutely beyond the scope of
many players. It's not like Magic with it's professional players, who
can afford to go internationally, but I can't say I know more then 2
people who can afford to such a thing.
The reason why this is so harsh for Australia is that the main way
people get to the Nats is by carpool. We don't have our Nats tied in
with a Con, we go to the Nats just for Jyhad. And so, the only
affordable way many people can afford to go to the Nats is by
splitting costs. Now, not everyone who qualifies can or wants to go
to the Nats, and seeing as at least half the cities of Australia that
have held Qualifiers had less then 12 people going for it, 3 people do
NOT make a cross country carpool. Of the 7 cities, only one city was
within 10 hours of the next. We are EXTREMELY spread out.
Now, this may not seem bad to Americans or Europeans (I'm hoping to
get some support from the South Americans!) But the only people who
play VTES are in these capitol cities. To better explain, take the
South East Region of the USA. In size, less then 1/5 of the
continental USA. But there are more then 7 cities where people travel
from to play at the VTES Qualifiers, most with less then a 6 hour
drive or a $100 plane ticket. Here, the cities are the Qualifiers.
Some people have traveled up to 10 hours by car to go a qualifier
because there were not enough slots. But in the states, if you don't
make your own regional qualifier, it's not that far for many to go to
another.

What I'm basically trying to say is, by making it harder to
qualify(normally, the 50% qualify in a qualifer with less then 20, top
10 for qualifiers over 20), you are making it harder for those who do
qualify to make it to the Nats. Less people equals less interest.
Less interest means less people, which totally means less cards being
sold.

Please, for this small continent (smallest in the world! And only 20
million people in a nation about the size of the USA) can you please
make some exceptions to have more people qualify per qualifier. If
anything, to keep the game going, and its players happy.

Thanks,
Jamie
The Seppo

Dude, it's not like this is a free lunch kind of situation. The VTES
championship tournament series appears to exist as a promotional tool
for the game. We expect, then, that White Wolf wants it to be as
effective a promotional tool as possible. If changing the qualifying
rules makes the qualifier/championships in Australia become un-useful to
Australian VTES players, then it's not going to promote the game very
well for them, is it?

As I understand it, the change to the 25% rule (and the omission of
already-qualified players in calculations) is intended both to increase
the number of qualifying spots for large tournaments (eg the 170-player
last-chance European qualifier last year) and to slightly decrease the
number of spots from 50% for small tournaments (since it seems to have
been seen as "too easy" with the "count already-qualified players"
method that was in use last year).

It's only very recently that there even *existed* a qualifier system for
VTES championships - until I think three years ago, the "national" or
"North American" championship tournaments (at GenCon US for example)
were open events; all you had to do was show up. Now, obviously,
limiting qualifiers to the top 25% of finishers should produce a "more
competitive" (for some values of competitive) championship tournament
than the previous top 50% (for small tournaments). But it's not
necessarily going to be *much* more competitive, and it's not a priori
obvious that 50% is too high a percentage.

And why the whining about people whining? I understand that you don't
consider always staying polite on usenet to be a worthwhile use of your
time. But I can't really say I understand why. Sure, the newsgroup
doesn't *have* to be a welcoming or friendly or polite place for it to
be useful to some people. But it might be useful to more people if it
were. It's not your job to make it that way, of course, and it's your
right to say what you want. But I doubt that it ever helps anything to
insult people in public. Even if it is "just usenet" and even if you do
think they were asking for it. :-)

Josh

Messages.Author: the_capuchin
Messages.Body:
TOP TEN countries in numbers of players, provided by Damnans:

> United States___2240 North America
> Spain___________924 Europe
> Canada__________686 North America
> France__________527 Europe
> Brazil__________370 South America
> United Kingdom__307 Europe
> Sweden__________273 Europe
> Australia_______276 Oceania
> Italy___________277 Europe
> Germany_________248 Europe

I'm really surprised about this.
I knew we had more registered players in Brazil than one should
expect, but I didn't knew we surpassed UK, Sweden, Italy etc.

But just to clarify some things about the Brazilian case (since most
South American players are from here):

- I can safely say that more than 1/3 of our 370 players are located
in two major areas, Sao Paulo and Rio. That's 20 and 10 million people
cities with many advantages to promote the game if compared to rest of
the country (better wages, distribution, more stores etc.)

- This is a very large country, comprising a big portion of the whole
continent. Driving from some specific domains to the most distant ones
require a two-DAYS trip or even more if you're going on bus. So, even
carpooling isn't an option. if one wants to attend a Nats or a
Continental Championship here, he must be able to pay for an airplane
ticket. Other factors add to that:

- most VTES players I know, at least on Sao Paulo and Curitiba (where
I've played thus far), are regular professionals with their jobs. Only
a few are still at college. This means two things: first, most players
can't afford to leave their jobs for three or four days to travel and
attend a tournament, unless it's held on holidays; second, VTES is a
little too expensive hobby for us Brazilians.
Maybe it isn't a fair picture of the whole country (it's easier for me
to know more about Atlanta scene than, let's say, the Fortaleza
metagame, because I've never traveled to either but at least Atlanta
players show up on this forum), but AFAIK, you need to be an
established individual to even consider buying himself more than a few
starters around here. Thus, I believe many of these 370 registered
players are occasional ones, who started buying VTES and quit the game
too soon.

So, if one looks at it closer, it seems that costs and distance are
valid issues for us, but personal priorities are of major concern too.
So I can understand Jamie's "whinings" since we have the very same
problems, but Derek is right in one thing: changing the rules of the
qualifying system won't help that much as it seems to. We're trying to
find solutions to this, and I've even considered trying sponsorship to
pay the airplane tickets for the qualified players, but it isn't that
easy for a country where even M:TG was not that widespread to the
'mainstream' media until two or three years ago. How we are supposed
to be able to attract sponsorship, and prove it could be profitable,
when most local regular johns don't even know *what* a cardgame is?

This is our situation, I believe. I accepted the "job" as the
country's NC because I felt I should contribute to change that
perspective, and because the game, against all odds, is getting bigger
recently, so it isn't a lost cause. But Jamie, maybe the Brazilians
(can't say nothing for Chile and Argentina) didn't complain as much as
you about the new qualifying system because in fact it doesn't matter
that much to us. We haven't had the organization and savvy to run even
a single edition of a regular National Championship yet. But if I
believed it would matter that much, I'd let it be discussed on the
Conclave list and use the forum to debate alternative ways to run a
Nats or Continental Championship. For example, do you Princes
worldwide try attracting some kind of sponsorship for anything? (that
includes travel and hosting)

This is where I understand Derek's approach, though I don't think it
was necessary to play the harsh-truth yelder. The world isn't fair,
sure, but WW, V:EKN, the Princes and players worldwide do not have to
hold on their breaths because of what happens here and take measures
and exceptions to us. I do expect some flexibility from WW since they
know we're at the same side - i.e., promoting the game - but it's just
not practical to hold different systems to accomodate different
realities, at least not now. If only WW had branches worldwide... But
the new WoD has not hit the shelves and sold 20 million copies yet ;)

This said, I expect this flame war to end as soon as possible, if not
for peace, at least to leave room for debating practical solutions.

cheers,

the_capuchin
